title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6977 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China publishes its daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time the previous evening), and the number has become one of the most closely followed signals in Asian currency markets. Its importance has grown over the past month as Beijing has moved from holding back the yuan's rise to steering it gradually higher. --- Earlier: Weeeknd: EU plans 350,000 annual cap on Chinese hybrids after Beijing agrees 16-point deal --- Under China's managed float, the onshore yuan may trade up to 2% either side of the midpoint set each morning. The central bank arrives at that midpoint by weighing the previous session's close, moves in the US dollar and other major currencies, wider global FX conditions, and domestic priorities including capital flows, growth and financial stability. Because the calculation leaves room for judgement, the fixing doubles as a tool for shaping expectations. Once the rate is published, onshore trading proceeds within the band. If pressure drives the yuan toward either limit, the PBOC can respond by buying or selling the currency directly, adjusting liquidity, or acting through state-owned banks. That is why markets treat the fixing as a statement of intent. A midpoint stronger than forecast usually signals resistance to depreciation, while a weaker one can point to acceptance of a softer yuan, or discomfort with how quickly it is gaining. For close to a year, the second message prevailed.

title: Senegal Inflation Rate Eases to 1% in September
body: Senegal's annual inflation rate eased to 1.0% in September 2026, down from August's three-month high of 1.2%. The slowdown was mainly driven by a deceleration in food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation, the largest component of the consumer basket, which fell to 0.9% from a four-month high of 1.4% in August. Price growth also moderated in several other categories: transport (1.2% vs 1.7% in August), alcoholic beverages and tobacco (12.0% vs 12.6%), restaurants and hotels (1.8% vs 2.2%), and financial services (1.0% vs 1.1%). Inflation remained unchanged for recreation, sports and culture (0.8%), education (1.0%), and clothing and footwear (1.1%). In contrast, furnishings inflation edged up (0.7% vs 0.6%), while housing and utilities returned to positive territory (0.1% vs -0.9%). On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 1.1% in September, down from a 2.0% increase in August, when monthly inflation reached its highest level since July 2023. title: What is earnings season and why the first companies to report are important to watch
body: Four times a year, publicly traded companies release their financial results, giving investors a picture of how businesses are performing, whether conditions are improving or deteriorating, and whether current stock prices are justified by future profit expectations. For investors, earnings are about comparing actual results with expectations, assessing what management expects in the coming quarters, and determining whether the new information changes the outlook for future earnings. What is earnings season? Earnings season is a specific multi-week period each quarter when a vast majority of publicly traded companies cluster together to release their official financial earning (revenue, profits, and losses) and reports for the previous quarter. In the United States, it typically takes place four times a year, following the end of each fiscal quarter. The main reporting periods generally fall in January and February, April and May, July and August, and October and November. The exact timing varies by company because businesses have different fiscal calendars and reporting deadlines. During these periods, companies publish their quarterly earnings reports, which usually include an income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, comparisons with previous periods, and management commentary. Many companies also hold earnings calls, where executives explain the results and answer questions from analysts and investors.

title: Market playbook: What if US CPI comes in hot but stocks refuse to fall?

And all of that is made even more crucial as Treasury yields are threatening multi-decade highs in the past week or so. The usual expectation is that a hotter-than-expected inflation report will be bad news for stocks. But what if we actually get that but Wall Street refuses to play ball and stocks do not happen to fall? That is a rather interesting scenario, no? To start, let's just consider what the typical market reaction should be. Higher inflation would mean that the Fed might have to keep interest rates "higher for longer" or even raise them further to deal with stronger price pressures in general. As things stand, Fed funds futures are currently pricing in roughly an 81% probability that the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged later this month. As such, a hotter-than-expected inflation report could challenge that pricing expectations and see traders push for bets on another rate hike. If not, it could at least reinforce expectations of another move in December. In turn, that rightfully should translate to higher Treasury yields and a stronger dollar. And for stocks, that's usually not a good combination to deal with.

While much of the usual focus will be on whether the banks manage to beat earnings expectations, there is perhaps a more important story running in the background this time around. That being how the recent surge in Treasury yields is impacting the banking sector and, by extension, the broader US economy. Now, higher interest rates and yields aren't necessarily a bad thing for banks to begin with. They can charge more interest on loans and that potentially means fatter margins to work with in trying to earn more money. However, there's also the other side of the equation to be mindful about. Higher borrowing costs are also likely to weigh more on demand conditions, in particular demand for loans. Just think about businesses deciding to hold back on expansion plans or households putting off from taking up a new mortgage because financing has become too expensive. As such, that will be one of the key things to watch in the earnings reports this week. Besides that, banks will also have to face higher funding costs as they may need to offer better deposit rates to keep customers from moving their money elsewhere. So even if lending income improves, that doesn't automatically translate to better profit margins. And then there's also the question of credit quality.

title: Early Ethereum Foundation ETH recipients move $11M to Kraken: what the data shows
body: Early Ethereum Foundation ETH recipients move $11M to Kraken: what the data shows Two wallets that received Ether (ETH) from an early Ethereum Foundation distribution sent 4,393 ETH, worth about $11.1 million, to the Kraken exchange on Monday, according to on-chain tracker Lookonchain. The transfers prompted questions on social media about whether the Foundation is selling again. The wallet history on Arkham Intelligence supports a more cautious reading: the coins are two steps removed from the Foundation, and an exchange deposit is not the same as a sale. What the wallet trail shows Arkham data shows the Ethereum Foundation sent 59,751 ETH to an intermediary address about a decade ago, when ETH traded near $0.90. That address later split the coins into three parcels of roughly 18,000 ETH each and sent them to separate wallets, at a time when ETH was worth about $2.13. One of those three wallets made the largest of Monday's deposits, about 2,998 ETH, or around $7.6 million. Based on Lookonchain's total, the second wallet accounts for roughly 1,395 ETH. None of the downstream addresses is labelled as a Foundation wallet on Arkham. Equal parcels fit a pattern of ETH being distributed to separate recipients, but the data does not show who controls the wallets. This is also not the first time the main wallet has used Kraken. Roughly five years ago it sent about 4,000 ETH to Kraken deposit addresses, in batches of 1,000 and 2,000 ETH.

title: Fed's Hammack: Treasury rates are "modest" by historical standards
body: Comments from the Fed's Hammack cross the wires: Treasury rates right now are "modest" by historic standards. If the economy were to return to a 3% home mortgage it would likely mean something had gone wrong in the economy. The neutral rate is likely higher but it is hard to pin down. Hearing "early warning signs" of a possible problem with inflation expectations. Need to "cool the economy at the margins." Higher interest rates won't dissuade hyperscalers, but might influence firms in other industries. The question for the Fed now is how fast to make policy more restrictive. Don't want to threaten the jobs side of the Fed's mandate. There is more restraint that is needed; if monetary policy does nothing market conditions would change. Comments from low income workers was first about trading down, now they are beginning to juggle what bills to pay. Analysis: The message is hawkish. Hammack is framing the debate around how quickly to make policy more restrictive. Her concern about inflation expectations is key. If households and businesses begin to expect persistently higher inflation, bringing inflation back down could become more difficult. However, she also recognizes the balancing act. Lower-income workers are struggling to pay bills, and she does not want to threaten jobs. For traders, the comments lean toward tighter policy, but leave the pace unresolved.

title: NZDUSD sellers press toward key lows. Can they break through?

title: Gold falls toward hourly moving averages. Can sellers keep control?
body: Gold has rotated lower after reaching a session high of $4,217.19, falling short of the October 2 high at $4,226.83. The price subsequently fell to $4,154.79 and is currently trading near $4,167, down $27.50, or 0.65%. Reports that Kazakhstan has begun selling gold are attracting attention, while the higher Treasury-yield backdrop is also being cited as a headwind. Ironically, the US treasury market is closed today for the Columbus Day holiday. So although yields are higher, blaming it on higher yields today is kind of a stretch. Nevertheless, gold pays no interest. When Treasury yields rise, investors can earn more from holding government debt, increasing the opportunity cost of holding gold. That can weigh on demand, although the relationship does not work perfectly every day. Put the Kazakhstan headline in perspective The World Gold Council's September report showed that gold accounted for approximately 75% of Kazakhstan's reserves. It also showed that the country had accumulated 29 tonnes through July. With that much of its reserves concentrated in gold, some diversification would be understandable. That is a possible explanation, rather than confirmation of the reason for any current sales. One country selling does not establish a broader central-bank selling trend. The size, timing and purpose of the sales matter. My take? The headline is another ingredient in the pot that determines price.

title: Why winning more trades doesn't always make you a profitable trader
body: If someone walks up to you and says that they have more winning trades than they do losing ones, you would think that they are probably making bank. I mean, it sounds perfectly logical, no? If you're getting most of your trades right, then it makes sense that you should be making money. But what if I told you that winning more trades doesn't necessarily mean that you would be making money? It sounds convoluted now but that's where understanding your win rate and how that ties to risk/reward becomes important. If you're winning more than you are losing, that means you should have a win rate of over 50% in your trades. It can be something like 60% or maybe even higher like 80%. However, a high win rate doesn't automatically mean that you're going to be a profitable trader. The more important part of the equation to consider is arguably how much money are you actually making when you win compared to how much money are you losing when the trade goes bad. To make things easier to understand, let's go back to the apple store example again from our previous educational posts (yes, I love my apples). Just imagine you are buying apples from a supplier and then selling them to customers, hoping to make a tidy profit along the way. And let's say out of every 10 apple sales, you manage to make money on 6 of them. That's a win rate of 60%. Sounds decent enough, no? But here's the catch. Suppose you make $3 in profit on each successful apple sale.

title: OPEC cuts oil demand forecast sharply as supply risks keep prices elevated
body: OPEC has just announced a rather significant downgrade to its oil demand outlook for this year. The bloc slashed its growth forecast to just 400,000 bpd, down from the 1.4 million bpd it had projected at the start of the year. Now, that's quite a substantial revision to say the least. According to OPEC secretary general, Haitham Al Ghais, the latest downgrade reflects the developments in the oil market throughout the year. And they are also still expecting some of that deferred demand to materialise some time in 2027. In other words, OPEC is anticipating that there will be a recovery in consumption conditions next year. Having said that, the present outlook is arguably the more pressing issue for oil traders. Despite the weaker demand outlook, prices are still keeping elevated with Brent crude seen above $105 and WTI crude trading back above $92 today. That's largely due to the ongoing tensions in the Middle East, which are continuing to keep supply risks firmly in the picture. The latest attacks on oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi strike on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport over the weekend serve as a timely reminder that tensions are still running high. And that means the oil market will have to be cautious as disruptions to shipping flows could worsen further at any time. It's one thing to have less demand for oil but it is a whole other thing when supply is still struggling to get to where it needs to go.

title: Connecting the dots: Following the money behind the AI boom on Wall Street
body: Just about everyone wants a piece of the AI pie these days. Tech companies are spending big and investors are dreaming even bigger. It seems like nobody wants to miss out. With billions of dollars being poured into AI, there is a lot of money to go around and also to be made - or at least that is what everyone is hoping for at the end of the day. But the main question remains, where exactly is all this money going? For the most part, you have your big tech giants spending heavily on building data centers and buying up powerful chips in order to run their respective AI services. And that means the companies that are supplying all this equipment are among the first to benefit from the spending boom. Yup, those are the likes of Nvidia and TSMC for example. The former designs advanced chips while the latter manufactures them. And so the more money that is being spent on AI infrastructure, the greater the potential demand for their products and services. In turn, that potentially translates to higher sales and bigger profits - which investors will look to bet on in the stock market. I would say that is arguably the more straightforward part. The other part is one that is more tricky to navigate as it doesn't just involve how much money that all of these companies are making today. It's about pricing in how much they could potentially earn in the years ahead.

title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, October 13, 2026 - RBA minutes due
body: Two releases this week will shape expectations for the Reserve Bank of Australia's next move: the minutes of its September policy meeting, due Tuesday, and Thursday's September labour force figures. Both come out at 11:30 am Sydney time, 00:30 GMT (8:30 pm ET the previous evening). Today we get the minutes. In September, the RBA's Monetary Policy Board raised the cash rate by a quarter point to 4.60%. The decision was unanimous and widely expected, and it was the fourth increase of the cycle. The board said inflation was still too high, reflecting strain on domestic capacity as well as global shocks from the Middle East conflict and the AI investment boom. It acknowledged that the economy was slowing and the jobs market easing. Neither was happening fast enough to return inflation to target within a reasonable timeframe, it said, particularly with oil prices under renewed upward pressure. CBA says the minutes should show how seriously the board considered keeping rates on hold. It will also be looking for whether they echo the softer tone Governor Michele Bullock struck at her press conference, when she stressed that the four hikes would take time to work through the economy. The bank sees a higher bar for further tightening. Westpac takes a firmer view and forecasts another increase, to 4.85% by December. The September hike has already weighed on households.

title: Tension in the releases sent crude oil prices to a new high
body: Buyers regain control, with $93.48 now a key level to hold. Crude oil pushed to its highest level since late September, with reports of increased Middle East tensions helping fuel the rally. A technical break above a key swing area gave buyers another reason to push higher. On the hourly chart, the price moved above resistance between $92.29 and $93.48, reaching a high of $94.36 before rotating lower. The current price is near $93.56, with the pullback so far holding above the top of that former resistance area. That makes $93.48 the immediate risk-defining level for buyers. When resistance is broken, traders want to see it hold as support. Stay above, and the upside remains the path of least resistance. Move back below, and the breakout loses some of its bullish appeal, opening the door for a deeper rotation into the swing area. The next upside targets come in at: $94.36: Today's high. $96.50–$97.00: Swing highs from late September. $98.48: Another higher swing high. Earlier in the session, the picture was much different. Crude fell to $89.61, briefly moving below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages. However, downside momentum quickly faded, and the price snapped back above both averages. The sellers had their shot. They could not sustain the break. Buyers took back control, with the hourly price action since then showing a largely steady climb. The broader technical picture also helped set the stage for the rebound.

title: EURUSD dips to a new low going back to May 2025
body: The EURUSD has extended below last week's low of 1.11603, reaching 1.1155 today—its lowest level since May 2025. The pair is currently trading near 1.1159. The sellers got their opening earlier today when the rally stalled at 1.1217, near the falling 100-hour moving average at the time (see blue line on the chart above). The buyers had their shot, but they could not get above that technical ceiling. The subsequent move to a new low keeps the sellers in control. What comes next on the downside? The next key target is 1.11296, the 50% midpoint of the rally from the January 2025 low to the January 2026 high. A swing low from mid-May is also near that level, making it an important area to watch. For beginner traders, that convergence matters: two technical reference points identify the same area where buyers may look to lean against support and define their risk. A break below—and the ability to stay below—would open the door toward 1.1060, the May 2025 low, with limited support in between. What would give buyers more hope? The first step would be a move back above the falling 100-hour moving average, currently near 1.12056 (blue line on the hourly chart at the top of the post). That would ease some of the immediate downside pressure, but buyers would still need to get and stay above the falling 200-hour moving average near 1.12308. The price has not traded above that longer moving average since September 10, when EURUSD was near 1.1610.
